blocks.heading: Location depends on the activity
blocks.text: Location factors include access to customers, suppliers, labour and skills, transport, premises, utilities, communications, land cost and relevant public conditions. Explain why a factor matters to the particular activity instead of listing inputs alone. Heavy materials may make transport cost decisive for a manufacturer, while a convenience retailer needs customer access. A service may need either face-to-face footfall or reliable remote communication. Cheaper rent can be outweighed by lost sales or unreliable supplies. Rank the most consequential constraints and compare realistic alternatives.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Tula Fresh Foods compares a cheap isolated site with a more expensive site near customers and reliable delivery routes. The cheaper site may raise transport time and spoilage risk and reduce customer access. Compare total practical consequences rather than rent alone.

blocks.heading: Manufacturing location
blocks.text: A manufacturer transforms inputs and often needs appropriate premises, utilities, labour skills and transport links to suppliers and markets. Bulky inputs or products can make freight important; perishability can make reliable quick access decisive. The relative importance depends on the product and process. A cheap site without sufficient power or delivery access may not support reliable production.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Nela Blocks makes heavy building blocks for nearby construction sites. Road access and distance to customers affect delivered cost because the output is bulky. An attractive rent alone cannot settle the location.

blocks.heading: Retail location
blocks.text: A retailer supplies final customers and often depends on convenient access, suitable footfall, parking or delivery links, nearby competitors and premises cost. High footfall is useful only if it includes likely buyers and the extra sales can justify the rent. Online retail changes access needs but still requires fulfilment and suitable communication.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Ota Snacks compares a busy commuter route with a cheap site far from its intended buyers. Relevant passing customers can support convenience sales, while the remote rent saving may be outweighed by lower demand. Check actual target footfall rather than total pedestrians alone.

blocks.heading: Service location
blocks.text: A service business’s location needs depend on how it serves customers. A walk-in repairer may need accessible local premises, while a remote administrative service may depend more on connectivity and skilled staff. Urgency, face-to-face contact, transport and trust can be decisive. Do not apply the same ranking to every service or assume online delivery removes all location costs.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Eya Emergency Repairs must reach local customers quickly with suitable equipment. Nearby skills and short journeys support its promised response. A distant cheap office would not provide that capability by itself.

blocks.heading: Keeping the ideas apart
blocks.text:
Explain why “labour and land” alone is not enough to justify Omi Repairs choosing a site near customers.

Labour and land are factor inputs. A location explanation identifies why this site provides suitable skills, premises or customer access at an acceptable cost. For urgent repairs, proximity can shorten response time; naming inputs without linking them to the site does not explain the choice.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Production method, scale and location
blocks.text:
Nara Cabinets receives varied custom orders requiring local measurement. It has skilled workers and suitable local premises. It compares job production near customers with a distant standard flow line whose lower stated rent is offset by slow customer contact. For part (b) only, demand changes to a dependable large contract for identical cabinets delivered on a non-urgent schedule; individual local measurement is no longer required. Other facts remain unchanged.

a Evaluate Nara’s method and site combination under the original facts. [12]
b Evaluate it after demand changes to the stated standard contract. Explain whether the recommendation should change. [12]

a Local job production matches individual specifications and measurement access. A distant standard line does not solve those needs and may sit underused; lower rent is insufficient. Prefer local flexibility despite its labour requirement. b The standard non-urgent contract removes individual measurement and strengthens the case for flow at a suitable site. Because the contract is for a fixed quantity, batch production of the identical cabinets may give most of the repetition savings without committing to a continuous flow line; flow is justified only if similar large orders are expected to continue. Dependable volume can use capacity, though coordination, breakdown and other diseconomies may offset expected unit savings. Distance is less harmful when delivery is not urgent, but compare transport, equipment investment, skills and contract duration before moving. The original method preference weakens; investigate flow and the alternative site rather than approve automatically. The decision changes with volume, variety and access needs, not with a universal ranking of methods.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Production method, scale and location
blocks.text:
Eha Gates makes custom gates for nearby households. Each order has different dimensions. Skilled workers and suitable premises are available locally. A foreign site offers lower rent but would delay measuring and installation, which customers require quickly. No large standard contract exists.

a Explain how production method and location should jointly fit Eha’s customer requirements. [8]
b Evaluate whether a move to a distant standard operation is justified by lower rent alone. [12]

a Job production supports varied dimensions with skilled work; proximity permits quick measurements and installation. A standard flow line and delayed contact conflict with those requirements despite possible capacity. The selected method and site therefore reinforce the same custom-service offer. b Lower rent saves one cost, but delays can lose customers and standardisation can make the output unsuitable. A flow line’s potential unit-cost savings require sufficient standard demand, capacity use and coordination costs that do not offset them; those conditions are not established. Retain the local custom operation and review if demand changes. Do not infer a sound move merely from one cheap input or assume a large machine guarantees efficiency.
